newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: News report throws Philippine markets into frenzy.
newsitem.headline: News report throws Philippine markets into frenzy.

text.p: Fresh rumours that the Philippines was thinking of devaluing its currency, furiously denied by officials, threw Manila's financial markets into a tailspin on Wednesday.
The Philippine stock market took one of its steepest falls in three months and the Central Bank had to sell up to $300 million to defend the peso.

The latest flurry followed an interview in the Singapore Straits Times with Trade and Industry Minister Cesar Bautista reporting him as saying devaluation would be discussed at a Monetary Board meeting on Wednesday.

Both Bautista and Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson denied the report, and insisted Manila was sticking to a policy which has kept the peso almost unchanged against the dollar in well over a year.
On Tuesday, the International Monetary Fund praised Philippine authorities for the way they have handled the almost relentless attacks on its currency, especially in the past two weeks.

But whatever the accuracy of the newspaper report, and however valid the argument that Philippine economic fundamentals are sound, traders said the latest market reaction underscored how nervous investors had become about the peso's prospects.
The focus of their worries is that the Philippines has been tainted by Thailand's financial crisis, which resulted in a de facto devaluation last week.

"The market is very jittery. It believes there may be some truth in these peso devaluation rumours. Overseas investors, who took positions in the peso believing it would be strong, are panicking," the treasurer at one leading foreign bank said.

"All these comparisons between the Philippines if looked at closely show the resemblance is not so close, but since we are in the same region and an emerging market we are caught in all these uncertainties," he said.
Share prices slumped over four percent in morning trade, the sharpest fall since April when the market was also battered by fears of a spillover from the financial problems in Thailand.
The peso also came under renewed pressure from speculators, forcing the Central Bank to dump at least $300 million.
Earlier this week, again in response to an article in the Singapore Straits Times and also denied by officials, the Central Bank pushed interest rates to their highest in 2-1/2 years.

Analysts said the peso defensive measures are beginning to take their toll, and that high interest rates, if they go on too long, will start to hurt industry in the Philippines, which hopes to become Asia's next economic tiger.
Bankers said that so far the peso is probably safe.
"Speculators can't drive it," Bank of America global capital markets managing director in Manila, Jaime Panganiban said.
The danger, though, could come from major companies, both local and international, if they start to lose their nerve.
One sign would be if they switched their loans from dollars to pesos. If there are prospects of a devaluation it would make more sense to do loans in pesos.
"So far, I haven't seen that. There hasn't been any wave of alarm from local conglomerates," Panganiban said.
